# Containerizing a Single-Container Node.js App

In the modern DevOps ecosystem, **containerization** has become a core practice for deploying and running applications efficiently across environments. Whether you're working locally, on a VM, or in the cloud, Docker enables you to package everything your app needs to run—code, dependencies, libraries, configuration—into a **single, portable unit**: the **container**.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2025/images/image.png)

## Lab Overview

In this lab, we’ll dive into containerizing a simple **Node.js** application using **Docker**. You’ll learn how to:

- Write and understand a `Dockerfile`
- Build and tag a Docker image
- Run your app inside a Docker container
- Push your image to Docker Hub (optional)
- Understand and inspect Docker layers
- Optimize images using **multi-stage builds**

## Step 1: Understanding Concepts Before You Code

### What is Containerization?

**Containerization** is the process of packaging an application and its dependencies into a container image. This image can be run anywhere, ensuring consistency across different systems.

### What is a Dockerfile?

A **Dockerfile** is a simple text file that contains instructions for building a Docker image. Each line in the Dockerfile creates a new **layer** in the final image.

## Step 2: Creating the Node.js App

Let’s begin by creating a simple Node.js web server.

```bash
mkdir my-node-app
cd my-node-app
```

Now create a file named `app.js` and paste the following code:

```javascript
const http = require('http');

const hostname = '0.0.0.0';
const port = 8000;

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.statusCode = 200;
  res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain');
  res.end('Hello, World!\n');
});

server.listen(port, hostname, () => {
  console.log(`Server running at http://${hostname}:${port}/`);
});
```

This server responds with “Hello, World!” when accessed on port 8000.

## Step 3: Writing the Dockerfile

Create a new file named `Dockerfile` in the same directory and add the following content:

```Dockerfile
# Use a lightweight official Node.js base image
FROM node:14-alpine

# Set working directory inside container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy the app source code
COPY app.js .

# Install the required module (http is built-in, this is just for demo)
RUN npm install http@0.0.1-security

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 8000

# Start the Node.js app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

**Why this works**: 

Every line in the Dockerfile builds upon the last, creating an efficient container image. Docker caches each layer to speed up future builds.

## Step 4: Building the Docker Image

In the terminal, build your Docker image:

```bash
docker build -t my-node-app:1.0 .
```

Once complete, verify the image exists:

```bash
docker images
```

**Expected output:**

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2025/images/image-1.png)

## Step 5: Running the Container

Run your app using:

```bash
docker run -d --name my-node-app-container -p 80:8000 my-node-app:1.0
```

- `-d`: Run in the background
- `--name`: Assigns a container name
- `-p 80:8000`: Maps your machine’s port 80 to the app’s port 8000

Check it’s running:

```bash
docker ps
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2025/images/image-2.png)

Now test the app:

```bash
curl http://localhost
```

You should see:

```
Hello, World!
```

## Step 6: (Optional) Push to Docker Hub

> Only do this if you have a Docker Hub account.

1. Login:

    ```bash
    docker login
    ```

2. Tag your image:

    ```bash
    docker tag my-node-app:1.0 your-docker-id/my-node-app:1.0
    ```

3. Push:

    ```bash
    docker push your-docker-id/my-node-app:1.0
    ```

Your image is now public on Docker Hub!

## Step 7: Understanding Docker Layers

Every Dockerfile instruction creates a layer. Inspect your image layers:

```bash
docker history my-node-app:1.0
```

You’ll see each command (FROM, COPY, RUN) listed with size info.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/refs/heads/main/Docker%20Labs/Lab%2025/images/image-3.png)

**Tip**: Layers are cached. If you change the last layer, only that one is rebuilt next time!

## Step 8: Optimizing with Multi-Stage Builds

Here's a more efficient Dockerfile using multi-stage builds:

```Dockerfile
# Stage 1: Build environment
FROM node:14-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY app.js .
RUN npm install http@0.0.1-security

# Stage 2: Production image
FROM node:14-alpine
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app .
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

Rebuild with:

```bash
docker build -t my-node-app:optimized .
```

This reduces final image size and excludes unnecessary dependencies from the build stage.

## Conclusion

By completing this lab, you now have a solid understanding of how to containerize a basic Node.js application. More importantly, you’ve learned **best practices** and **Docker fundamentals** that will scale as your applications grow.

This lab was just the beginning. As you dive deeper into Docker, try combining multiple containers, using Docker Compose, or deploying containerized apps to orchestration platforms like Kubernetes.
